title: Strict localizations are invariant under ind-etale morphisms
statement:
Let $u:T\to S$ be a morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme] which is ind-etale locally on source and target: near each point of $T$, choose affine opens $\operatorname{Spec}B\subset T$ and $\operatorname{Spec}A\subset S$ such that $u$ maps the first into the second and $B$ is a filtered colimit of etale $A$-algebras of finite presentation [def-weil-pbc-ind-etale-algebra]. For every geometric point $t:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to T$ [def-weil-geometric-point], with $s=u(t)$ defined using the same field $\Omega$, the canonical functorial map of strict localizations [lem-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-functoriality]
$$T_{(t)}\longrightarrow S_{(s)}$$
is an isomorphism over $S$. Strict localizations have the inverse-limit construction of [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit]. The assertion applies after arbitrary scheme base change [def-pc-fibre-product] of $u$ and includes the canonical structural map [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-structural-map] of a strict localization, localized again at its closed geometric point.

proof.text: Choose the affine charts $V=\operatorname{Spec}B\subset T$ and $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subset S$ in the hypothesis around the images of $t,s$. Put $H_S=\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{S,s}$ and $H_T=\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{T,t}$, using the small pointed-neighbourhood colimits in the strict-localization definition. That definition identifies their spectra with the stated inverse limits. Functoriality says both rings are strictly henselian local, their structural maps $j_S,j_T$ send closed points to the images of $s,t$, and the canonical map is $\operatorname{Spec}h$ for a local homomorphism $h:H_S\to H_T$ with $j_S\operatorname{Spec}h=uj_T$. Both structural maps factor through the chosen affine charts: their inverse images of these opens contain the closed point of the respective local spectrum, and an open containing the maximal ideal of a local ring is the whole spectrum. Indeed a basic neighbourhood $D(f)$ of that point has $f$ outside the maximal ideal, hence $f$ is a unit and $D(f)$ is the whole spectrum. Let $a:A\to H_S$ and $b:B\to H_T$ be the resulting ring maps. The displayed structural equality gives $ha=b\circ(A\to B)$: both corresponding spectrum maps factor through the open $U$, whose inclusion is a monomorphism; uniqueness of the ring map inducing an affine scheme morphism then gives the equality. Thus $h$ is an $A$-algebra map for precisely these structural algebra structures.

proof.text: Apply the affine-chart ind-etaleness lemma to $(S,s,U,H_S,a)$ and $(T,t,V,H_T,b)$, with the identity spectrum identifications. Its chart contains the respective geometric point and its required structural-map equality is exactly the factorization in step 1. It gives $A\to H_S$ and $B\to H_T$ ind-etale. Since $A\to B$ is ind-etale by hypothesis, stability under composition makes $A\to H_T$ ind-etale. Now $H_S,H_T$ are both ind-etale $A$-algebras, and $h$ is the $A$-algebra map checked in step 1. The relative-map clause of ind-etale stability therefore makes $h$ ind-etale, hence weakly etale. This uses no finite-presentation hypothesis on $B$ itself.

The map $h$ is local between local rings, its source $H_S$ is strictly henselian by functoriality, and step 2 proves it weakly etale. The weakly-etale strict-local theorem (Olivier) applies with $A=H_S$, $B=H_T$ and says $h$ itself is an isomorphism. Its inverse induces an inverse of $\operatorname{Spec}h$, by contravariant functoriality of spectrum. This is the prescribed canonical morphism, rather than an unspecified isomorphism, since $h$ was the functorial map from step 1. It is over $S$ by $j_S\operatorname{Spec}h=uj_T$; composing this equality with the inverse also verifies that the inverse is over $S$.

For arbitrary $g:S'\to S$ put $T'=T\times_SS'$ and take any geometric point $t'$ of $T'$, with projection $s'$ to $S'$. Choose $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ and $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ as in the original hypothesis around its projection to $T$. Choose an affine open $W=\operatorname{Spec}C$ about the image of $s'$ inside $g^{-1}(U)$. In $T'$ the intersection of the inverse images of $V\subset T$ and $W\subset S'$ is open and contains $t'$. The fibre-product universal property identifies this open with $V\times_UW$: a map into it is precisely a pair of maps to $V,W$ whose composites to $U$ agree, since $U\to S$ is a monomorphism. The affine fibre-product lemma identifies it with $\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_A C)$ and its map to $W$ with the spectrum of $C\to B\otimes_A C$. Ind-etale stability under base change makes this ring map ind-etale. Thus $T'\to S'$ satisfies exactly the original local affine hypothesis at every $t'$, without any finiteness or separation requirement on $g$. Apply the argument of steps 1--3 to this morphism and the geometric point $t'$ (using its same geometric field for $s'$). It gives the required canonical isomorphism of strict localizations after arbitrary base change.

Finally let $L=S_{(s)}=\operatorname{Spec}H_S$ with its canonical structural map $j:L\to S$. For an affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ containing the image of $s$, the local-spectrum argument of step 1 shows that the entire map $j$ factors through $U$. Applying the affine-chart ind-etaleness lemma with the identity $\operatorname{Spec}H_S=L$ gives $A\to H_S$ ind-etale. Thus $j$ satisfies the local affine hypothesis at every point of $L$, using the whole affine source $L$ and this one target chart. Functoriality, clause (1), gives the closed geometric lift $\widetilde s:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to L$ of $s$: it is induced by the residue map $H_S\to\kappa(s)^{\mathrm{sep}}\subset\Omega$, where the separable closure is taken inside the given geometric field. Apply steps 1--3 to $j$ and $\widetilde s$. Since $j\widetilde s=s$, the result is the canonical isomorphism $L_{(\widetilde s)}\to S_{(s)}=L$. This proves the localization-again clause for its specified closed geometric point. The inverse-limit construction used throughout is unchanged, being the definition in step 1.
